article_title: Rust Demotes 32-bit Windows Targets i686-pc-windows-msvc and i686-pc-windows-gnu to Std-Only Starting With Rust 1.100

content_preview.title: Rust Demotes 32-bit Windows Targets i686-pc-windows-msvc and i686-pc-windows-gnu to Std-Only Starting With Rust 1.100
content_preview.summary: Starting with Rust 1.100.0, the compiler team will stop shipping host tools for two 32-bit Windows targets, leaving only the standard library and requiring cross-compilation.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

The Rust project will stop distributing the compiler for 32-bit Windows hosts. According to the [Rust Blog](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/10/02/demoting-i686-windows-targets-to-std-only/), "With Rust 1.100.0, the following changes to 32-bit Windows targets will happen:" the `i686-pc-windows-msvc` target moves from Tier 1 with host tools to Tier 1 without host tools, and `i686-pc-windows-gnu` moves from Tier 2 with host tools to Tier 2 without host tools. The post, dated October 2,...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear Briefing (499 words, within 300-800). Overview states the exact tier changes; What Changes explains the practical consequence; Stated Reasons separates blog rationale from RFC arguments; What We Don't Know is honest. Title term 'Std-Only' matches the Rust Blog's own 'std-only' terminology.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all three snapshots from disk (gunzip). source-0.html.gz (blog.rust-lang.org, 'Demoting i686 Windows targets to std-only', Oct. 2, 2026, Mateusz Mikula and Ralf Jung on behalf of the Compiler team): confirms verbatim 'With Rust 1.100.0, the following changes to 32-bit Windows targets will happen:'; 'i686-pc-windows-msvc Tier 1 with host tools target will be demoted to Tier 1 without host tools'; 'i686-pc-windows-gnu Tier 2 with host tools target will be demoted to Tier 2 without host tools'; 'Builds of the standard library will continue to be distributed, but host tools such as the compiler will be no longer available'; 'i686-pc-windows-msvc as a Tier 1 target still undergoes CI testing'; cross-compiling from a still-supported host (such as 64-bit Windows) required; 'After Rust 1.100, it will no longer be possible to install toolchains on 32-bit Windows hosts'; 'Other 32-bit platforms are not impacted'; 'For the time being, the prebuilt standard library is still available'; the 15-years / October 2025 rationale; 'encountered compiler binaries crashing when built with the i686 MSVC target, and the GNU C++ toolchain failing with OOMs during LLVM build'; pointers to RFC 3999 and MCP 1020. The snapshot is the real dated post (URL /2026/10/02/, HTTP 200). No release date for Rust 1.100 appears in the post or in any source, and the article gives none. source-1.html.gz (RFC 3999 text, 3999-std-only-i686-msvc.md): confirms Start Date 2026-07-02, RFC PR rust-lang/rfcs#3999, Datadog-sourced download counts (i686-pc-windows-msvc 432k rustc / 6.75M std; x86_64-pc-windows-msvc 34.33M / 20.85M; i686-pc-windows-gnu 72k / 3.57M), the quote 'receives far more downloads than its toolchain, because it is primarily used by cross-compiling' (RFC: 'std receives far more downloads than its toolchain, because it is primarily used by cross-compiling'), the 4GiB LTO quote verbatim, and that 32-bit x86 host toolchains are tested by running on a 64-bit host. source-2.html.gz (PR #3999): title 'Change i686-pc-windows-msvc from Tier 1 with host tools => Tier 1 without host tools', status Merged on Sep 1, 2026 (FCP finished), confirming the article's 'shown as merged'. The RFC text covers only i686-pc-windows-msvc; the article correctly attributes the GNU demotion to MCP 1020 per the blog. manifest suspicious_patterns is null for all three sources; nothing to adjudicate. blog.rust-lang.org, rust-lang.github.io and github.com are all on the allowlist (rust-lang.github.io is not used by this article).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every specific (tiers, 'without host tools' meaning, 1.100 version, dates, authors, RFC number/title/merged status, download figures, quotes) traces to a snapshot. The article does not call the RFC 'accepted'; it says the PR is shown as merged, which the PR page confirms. Rationale is limited to what the blog and RFC state; none invented. The internal cross-reference to the Rust 1.99 article resolves to src/content/articles/2026-10/03-rust-199-... (/article/2026-10/03-...). Minor note: calling 1.99 'the previous stable release' is an inference from the Herald's own 1.99 article (released Oct 1) rather than the three cited sources; low-risk context, not a claim about the demotion.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional; no editorializing or AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: No existing article covers i686 Windows targets or this demotion (grep of src/content/articles for i686 finds only an unrelated Copilot article). Only related prior item is the Rust 1.99 article, a different event.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, well-sourced Briefing with correct tier terminology, no invented release date, and correct RFC status. APPROVE.
